title: Astronomers have made a movie of four giant planets circling another star

cover.alt: A dark blue square with a black circle at its centre where a star’s light has been removed, and four faint white dots around it: the planets of HR 8799.
cover.credit: J. Wang/W. Thompson/C. Marois/Q. Konopacky · CC BY 4.0

body: HR 8799 is a young star about 133 light-years away in the constellation Pegasus, and in 2008 it became the first star seen to have **several planets in a direct photograph**. Its four gas giants, each several times heavier than Jupiter, orbit far from the star. Because they are young, they are still hot and bright in near-infrared light, which lets big telescopes pick them out next to the star’s glare. By photographing them again and again from 2009 to 2021, astronomers could watch the planets creep along their orbits; the outermost takes roughly 400 years to go round once.

slides.alt: Four small white dots move slowly anticlockwise around a black central circle on a dark blue background, with dates from 2009 to 2021 and a 20 au scale bar along the bottom.
slides.caption: A movie made from ten Keck Observatory images of HR 8799 taken from 2009 to 2021, slowed to half speed: the four planets inch around the masked star.
slides.credit: J. Wang/W. Thompson/C. Marois/Q. Konopacky · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt, slowed to half speed
slides.music: “Jellyfish in Space” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Planets are faint and sit right next to a dazzling star. How did astronomers first photograph these ones in 2008?
slides.detail: Adaptive optics undoes much of the blurring caused by Earth’s air. The Keck and Gemini telescopes caught three of the planets; the fourth turned up in 2009–2010.

slides.question: Why do HR 8799’s planets shine brightly enough in infrared to be photographed?
options: They are young and still hot
slides.explanation: HR 8799 is only about 42 million years old, and its planets are young enough to still be hot, so they glow brightly in near-infrared light.
